all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The superior/dorsal surface of the tongue displaying the terminal sulcus (sulcus terminalis) dividing it into the anterior two-thirds (oral part covered with filiform, fungiform, and vallate papillae) and the posterior one-third (pharyngeal part containing lingual tonsils).
all.keyConcept: Dorsum of tongue: Divided by the V-shaped sulcus terminalis into anterior 2/3 (presulcal, papillae-bearing) and posterior 1/3 (postsulcal, lymphoid follicles).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large fan-shaped extrinsic tongue muscle originating from the superior mental spine (genial tubercle) of the mandible and inserting into the body of the hyoid bone and along the entire length of the tongue from root to tip; acts to protrude and depress the tongue.
all.keyConcept: Genioglossus muscle: The 'safety muscle' of the tongue; innervated by CN XII (hypoglossal nerve), its bilateral contraction protrudes the tongue.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: U-shaped bone in the anterior neck at the C3 level, situated between the floor of the mouth and the thyroid cartilage; serves as an attachment site for suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles and the base of the tongue.
all.keyConcept: Hyoid bone: Suspended bone of the anterior neck that does not articulate with any other bone; supports the tongue and anchors laryngeal muscles.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Conical, muscular projection hanging down in the midline from the free posterior border of the soft palate; contains the musculus uvulae and assists in closing off the nasopharynx during swallowing.
all.keyConcept: Uvula: Muscular midline projection of the soft palate; innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X), deviation indicates vagal nerve lesion (deviates away from affected side).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Rigid bony partition forming the anterior two-thirds of the palate and roof of the oral cavity, formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae anteriorly and horizontal plates of the palatine bones posteriorly.
all.keyConcept: Hard palate: Bony roof of the mouth and floor of the nasal cavities; covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium bound firmly to periosteum.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Mobile, fibromuscular fold suspended from the posterior margin of the hard palate, extending posteroinferiorly into the pharynx to separate the nasopharynx from the oropharynx during swallowing.
all.keyConcept: Soft palate: Movable muscular fold consisting of muscle fibers, aponeurosis, lymphoid tissue, and mucous glands; elevated by tensor and levator veli palatini to seal the nasopharynx.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Thick, dense bone forming the lower jaw; the sagittal section demonstrates the symphysis menti and alveolar process supporting the lower dentition, providing inner attachment for the genial tubercles.
all.keyConcept: Mandible: Single lower facial bone articulating with the temporal bones at the TMJ; bears the lower teeth and anchors suprahyoid and masticatory muscles.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Paired facial bone forming the upper jaw; sagittal cross-section shows the alveolar process housing the maxillary incisors and palatine process contributing to the anterior hard palate.
all.keyConcept: Maxilla: Major bone of the upper face; forms parts of the floor of the orbits, lateral walls and floor of the nasal cavity, and the upper dental arch.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Fleshy muscular fold bounding the oral fissure superiorly, extending inferiorly from the base of the nose; contains the orbicularis oris muscle, labial glands, and is lined externally by skin and internally by mucous membrane.
all.keyConcept: Upper lip: Musculocutaneous upper boundary of the oral fissure; innervated sensory by the infraorbital nerve (V2) and motor by facial nerve (CN VII).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Fleshy muscular fold bounding the oral fissure inferiorly, separated from the chin by the labiomental sulcus; contains orbicularis oris muscle, covered by skin externally and non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium internally.
all.keyConcept: Lower lip: Inferior boundary of the oral fissure; innervated sensory by the mental nerve (branch of inferior alveolar nerve from V3) and motor by the facial nerve (CN VII).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Tag 1 indicates the inner lip of the ventral segment (anterior two-thirds) of the iliac crest. The muscle originating from the inner lip of the iliac crest (as well as the lateral one-third of the inguinal ligament, thoracolumbar fascia, and lower 6 costal cartilages) is the transversus abdominis muscle.
all.keyConcept: Transversus abdominis: Deepest flat abdominal muscle; originates from the inner lip of the iliac crest, lower six costal cartilages, thoracolumbar fascia, and lateral inguinal ligament.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Slit-like space of the oral cavity situated between the lips and cheeks externally, and the dental arches and gingivae internally; communicates with the exterior through the oral fissure (rima oris).
all.keyConcept: Oral vestibule (mouth vestibule): Peripheral space of the mouth outside the teeth; receives secretions from the parotid duct opposite the upper second molar tooth.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The circled middle subdivision of the pharynx, extending from the soft palate above to the superior border of the epiglottis below; communicates anteriorly with the oral cavity through the oropharyngeal isthmus and houses the palatine tonsils within the tonsillar sinuses.
all.keyConcept: Oropharynx: Middle pharyngeal compartment (C2–C3 level); common passage for food and air, lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and innervated sensory by CN IX.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The circled superior division of the pharynx, located posterior to the nasal cavities (choanae) and superior to the soft palate; contains the pharyngeal tonsils in its roof and the lateral pharyngeal openings of the auditory (Eustachian) tubes.
all.keyConcept: Nasopharynx: Exclusively respiratory chamber; lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium and innervated sensory by the maxillary nerve (V2/pharyngeal nerve).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Vertical mucous membrane fold on the lateral nasopharyngeal wall descending from the lower part of the tubal elevation (torus tubarius) towards the lateral wall of the pharynx, containing the salpingopharyngeus muscle.
all.keyConcept: Salpingopharyngeal fold: Overlies the salpingopharyngeus muscle; innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X) and acts to elevate the pharynx during swallowing.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Funnel-shaped triangular aperture on the lateral wall of the nasopharynx situated about 1–1.5 cm posterior to the inferior nasal concha; bounded superiorly and posteriorly by the tubal elevation (torus tubarius).
all.keyConcept: Pharyngeal orifice of auditory (Eustachian) tube: Connects the middle ear tympanic cavity with the nasopharynx to equalize atmospheric pressure across the tympanic membrane.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Prominent mucosal bulge on the lateral wall of the nasopharynx produced by the underlying cartilaginous end of the auditory (pharyngotympanic) tube, forming the superior and posterior margins of the tubal opening.
all.keyConcept: Tubal elevation (torus tubarius): Cartilaginous prominence of the auditory tube; anterior attachment for salpingopharyngeus and salpingopalatine folds, situated anterior to the pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenmüller).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Prominent vertical mucosal ridge (posterior pillar of the fauces) extending from the soft palate posteroinferiorly along the lateral wall of the pharynx behind the palatine tonsil; contains the palatopharyngeus muscle.
all.keyConcept: Palatopharyngeal arch: Posterior boundary of the tonsillar fossa overlying the palatopharyngeus muscle; innervated by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve (CN X).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Distinct curved mucosal fold (anterior pillar of the fauces) descending from the oral surface of the soft palate to the lateral border of the tongue immediately anterior to the tonsillar fossa; contains the palatoglossus muscle.
all.keyConcept: Palatoglossal arch: Anterior boundary of the tonsillar fossa and demarcation of the oropharyngeal isthmus; overlies palatoglossus muscle (innervated by CN X via pharyngeal plexus).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Subepithelial aggregation of lymphoid tissue embedded in the posterior wall and roof of the nasopharynx; when pathologically enlarged in children, it is known as adenoids and can obstruct nasal breathing and auditory tube function.
all.keyConcept: Nasopharyngeal tonsil (adenoid): Lymphoid collection forming the superior component of Waldeyer's tonsillar ring; covered by respiratory pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Ovoid lymphoid tissue mass occupying the tonsillar fossa on the lateral wall of the oropharynx, bounded anteriorly by the palatoglossal arch and posteriorly by the palatopharyngeal arch.
all.keyConcept: Palatine Tonsil (in tonsillar fossa): Primary lymphoid organ in the tonsillar fossa of the oropharynx, supplied by the tonsillar branch of the facial artery.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Small rounded anterior bony bar of the first cervical vertebra (atlas, C1) positioned directly in front of the odontoid process (dens of axis).
all.keyConcept: Anterior arch of atlas: Anterior segment of the ring of C1 lacking a vertebral body, articulating posteriorly with the dens of axis.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Prominent vertical tooth-like projection (odontoid process) arising superiorly from the body of the second cervical vertebra (axis, C2), situated immediately posterior to the anterior arch of atlas.
all.keyConcept: Dense of axis: Odontoid process of C2 acting as the pivot for rotational head movement at the atlantoaxial joint.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: First typical cervical vertebral body situated immediately inferior to the axis (C2), separated from it by the C2-C3 intervertebral disc.
all.keyConcept: 3rd Cervical vertebra: Typical cervical vertebra positioned directly below C2 (axis).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Muscular excretory duct arising from the anterior border of the parotid gland, crossing horizontally over the masseter muscle before piercing the buccinator.
all.keyConcept: Parotid duct (Stensen's duct): Traverses the masseter, pierces the buccinator, and opens into the oral cavity opposite the maxillary second molar.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Long excretory duct emerging from the deep lobe of the submandibular gland, coursing forward along the floor of the mouth medial to the sublingual gland.
all.keyConcept: Submandibular duct (Wharton's duct): Courses between mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles, crossed by the lingual nerve, to open at the sublingual caruncle.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Row of multiple tiny excretory duct orifices and conduits emerging from the sublingual gland along the crest of the sublingual fold.
all.keyConcept: Sublingual ducts (ducts of Rivinus): 8–20 small excretory ducts that drain the sublingual gland directly into the oral cavity along the plica sublingualis.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Smallest of the major salivary glands, situated submucosally in the floor of the mouth within the sublingual fossa of the mandible superior to the mylohyoid muscle.
all.keyConcept: Sublingual gland: Predominantly mucous-secreting salivary gland in the sublingual fossa of the mandible, innervated by CN VII via the chorda tympani.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large lobulated salivary gland located anteroinferior to the ear, occupying the retromandibular space superficial to the masseter and sternocleidomastoid muscles.
all.keyConcept: Parotid gland: Largest salivary gland; purely serous, enveloped by investing deep cervical fascia, and traversed by the facial nerve (CN VII).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Paired salivary gland located in the submandibular (digastric) triangle of the neck, wrapping around the posterior free border of the mylohyoid muscle.
all.keyConcept: Submandibular gland: Mixed seromucous gland in the digastric triangle responsible for the majority of baseline unstimulated saliva production.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: V-shaped shallow groove on the dorsum of the tongue running anterolaterally from the foramen caecum, separating the anterior two-thirds from the posterior one-third.
all.keyConcept: Sulcus terminalis: V-shaped landmark dividing the anterior oral tongue (presulcal, arch 1) from the posterior pharyngeal tongue (postsulcal, arches 3/4).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Small blind pit located at the median apex of the V-shaped sulcus terminalis on the dorsal surface of the tongue.
all.keyConcept: Foramen caecum: Nonfunctional midline pit at the sulcus terminalis apex marking the site of origin and descent of the embryonic thyroglossal duct.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Compact oval mass of lymphoid tissue situated laterally in the tonsillar sinus between the diverging palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
all.keyConcept: Palatine tonsils: Paired lymphoid aggregates situated between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches; key components of Waldeyer's lymphatic ring.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Aggregations of lymphoid nodules creating a cobblestone, irregular surface texture on the posterior one-third (pharyngeal surface) of the tongue behind the sulcus terminalis.
all.keyConcept: Lingual tonsils: Lymphoid nodules on the posterior third of the tongue innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); lack true crypts.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Thin, flexible leaf-like fibrocartilaginous structure situated posterior to the base of the tongue, forming the anterior boundary of the laryngeal inlet.
all.keyConcept: Epiglottis: Elastic fibrocartilage projecting behind the tongue base that folds over the laryngeal inlet to protect the airway during swallowing.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Anterior vertical mucosal fold extending inferiorly and laterally from the soft palate to the lateral border of the tongue, overlying the palatoglossus muscle.
all.keyConcept: Palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of fauces): Demarcates the boundary of the oropharyngeal isthmus; contains palatoglossus muscle innervated by CN X.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Elevated paired ridge of mucous membrane running anteromedially in the floor of the mouth on either side of the frenulum, produced by the underlying sublingual gland.
all.keyConcept: Sublingual fold (plica sublingualis): Mucosal elevation overlying the sublingual gland that bears the openings of the minor sublingual ducts.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Midline vertical sagittal fold of mucous membrane connecting the undersurface of the tongue to the floor of the mouth.
all.keyConcept: Lingual frenulum: Midline fold tethering the ventral tongue; congenitally short frenulum causes ankyloglossia (tongue-tie).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Smooth, thin, non-keratinized mucosal underside (ventral surface) of the tongue, visible when elevated, revealing the midline lingual frenulum and deep lingual veins.
all.keyConcept: Inferior surface of tongue: Non-papillated ventral tongue mucosa with visible deep lingual veins; ideal site for sublingual drug administration.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Four-way cruciate suture intersection on the oral surface of the hard palate formed by the perpendicular crossing of the median palatine suture and transverse palatine suture.
all.keyConcept: Cruciform suture: Cross-shaped junction between the median palatine and transverse palatine sutures uniting the maxillae and palatine bones.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Funnel-shaped midline opening/depression located in the anterior hard palate immediately posterior to the central maxillary incisors; transmits the nasopalatine nerve and terminal branches of the greater palatine vessels.
all.keyConcept: Incisive fossa: Midline anterior hard palate depression transmitting the nasopalatine nerve.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Smaller aperture located immediately posterior to the greater palatine foramen within the pyramidal process of the palatine bone; transmits the lesser palatine nerve and vessels to the soft palate.
all.keyConcept: Lesser Palatine Foramen: Located posterior to greater palatine foramen; transmits lesser palatine neurovascular bundle to soft palate.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large distinct foramen located at the posterolateral corner of the hard palate, medial to the third maxillary molar tooth, at the junction between the palatine process of the maxilla and horizontal plate of the palatine bone; transmits the greater palatine nerve and vessels.
all.keyConcept: Greater Palatine Foramen: Located medial to the 3rd maxillary molar; transmits greater palatine nerve and vessels to hard palate.

options: Greater Palatine nerve and Nasopalatine nerve
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Structures traversing the greater palatine foramen to supply the mucosa and glands of the hard palate and adjacent gingiva anteriorly up to the incisive fossa.
all.keyConcept: Greater Palatine Foramen contents: Transmits the greater palatine nerve and greater palatine vessels.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Neurovascular bundle passing through the lesser palatine foramen to distribute sensory fibers and blood supply to the soft palate and palatine tonsil.
all.keyConcept: Lesser Palatine Foramen contents: Transmits the lesser palatine nerve and vessels to supply the soft palate.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Traverses the incisive canal/fossa to communicate between the nasal cavity and the oral cavity, supplying the anterior portion of the hard palate (premaxilla).
all.keyConcept: Incisive fossa contents: Transmits the nasopalatine nerve and terminal branches of the greater palatine vessels.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Thin, firm fibrous sheet forming the skeletal framework of the soft palate, attached anteriorly to the posterior free border and posterior nasal spine of the horizontal plates of the palatine bones.
all.keyConcept: Palatine aponeurosis: Fibrous backbone of the soft palate attached to the posterior border of the hard palate.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Thin, concave posterior margin of the horizontal plate of the palatine bone that gives attachment to the palatine aponeurosis and marks the transition between the hard and soft palate.
all.keyConcept: Posterior border of hard palate: Free posterior edge giving attachment to the palatine aponeurosis.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Sharp median bony projection formed by the junction of the posterior borders of the horizontal plates of both palatine bones; gives origin to the musculus uvulae.
all.keyConcept: Posterior nasal spine: Sharp midline posterior projection giving origin to musculus uvulae.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Horizontal quadrilateral bony lamina that articulates anteriorly with the palatine process of the maxilla at the transverse palatine suture and meets its contralateral counterpart at the interpalatine suture to form the posterior third of the bony palate.
all.keyConcept: Horizontal plate of palatine bone: Forms posterior 1/3 of the hard palate.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Thick horizontal medial projection of the maxilla that meets the opposite side at the median palatine suture to form the anterior two-thirds of the hard palate.
all.keyConcept: Palatine process of maxilla: Forms the anterior 2/3 of the hard palate.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Slender vertical muscle arising from the scaphoid fossa and auditory tube whose tendon hooks around the pterygoid hamulus at a right angle to insert into the palatine aponeurosis; innervated by the mandibular nerve (CN V3).
all.keyConcept: Tensor veli palatini: Tenses soft palate; tendon hooks around pterygoid hamulus; innervated by CN V3.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Cylindrical muscle descending obliquely downwards and medially from the petrous temporal bone and auditory tube cartilage directly into the upper surface of the soft palate without winding around any bone; innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X).
all.keyConcept: Levator veli palatini: Elevates soft palate; descends directly into palate; innervated by CN X via pharyngeal plexus.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Smallest and most inferior cartilaginous/bony element of the sternum located in the epigastric fossa in the midline at the T9/T10 vertebral level.
all.keyConcept: Xiphoid process: Inferior end of sternum marking the infrasternal angle and level of T9/T10.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Point where the right linea semilunaris crosses the costal margin; lies at the level of the transpyloric plane (L1) and corresponds surface-anatomically to the fundus of the gallbladder.
all.keyConcept: Tip of 9th costal cartilage: Intersected by transpyloric plane and right linea semilunaris; overlies gallbladder fundus.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Fibrous cicatrix in the anterior abdominal midline resulting from the site of attachment of the umbilical cord; typically lies in the linea alba at the level of the intervertebral disc between L3 and L4 (T10 dermatome).
all.keyConcept: Umbilicus: Midline scar in linea alba; landmark for transumbilical plane and T10 dermatome.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Lower boundary of the thoracic cage formed by the cartilages of the 7th through 10th ribs curving obliquely downwards and laterally from the xiphisternal joint.
all.keyConcept: Costal margin: Sloping lower border of the thoracic wall formed by the 7th–10th costal cartilages.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Palpable superior curved bony margin of the ala of the ilium extending between the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS); highest point lies at the L4 vertebral level.
all.keyConcept: Iliac crest: Superior margin of ilium; highest point corresponds to the L4 supracristal plane.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Dense band formed by the rolled-under lower free border of the external oblique aponeurosis spanning from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic tubercle.
all.keyConcept: Inguinal ligament: Lower rolled-in border of external oblique aponeurosis between ASIS and pubic tubercle.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Curved shallow groove on the anterior abdominal wall marking the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, extending from the tip of the 9th costal cartilage to the pubic tubercle.
all.keyConcept: Linea semilunaris: Curved groove along the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Tagged midline groove/raphe running vertically along the anterior abdominal wall from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis, formed by the interlacing aponeurotic fibers of the abdominal obliques and transversus abdominis.
all.keyConcept: Linea alba: Fibrous midline abdominal raphe formed by decussation of bilateral abdominal wall aponeuroses extending from xiphoid to pubic symphysis.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Protrusion situated inferior (below) and lateral to the pubic tubercle, emerging below the inguinal ligament into the upper thigh through the femoral ring and canal.
all.keyConcept: Femoral hernia: Emerges inferior and lateral to the pubic tubercle, below the inguinal ligament, presenting as a mass in the femoral triangle.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Protrusion situated superior (above) and medial to the pubic tubercle, emerging above the inguinal ligament along the course of the inguinal canal.
all.keyConcept: Inguinal hernia: Emerges superior and medial to the pubic tubercle, above the inguinal ligament, passing through the inguinal canal.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Longitudinal anteroposterior anatomical section displaying the abdominal and pelvic cavities from the anterior abdominal wall to the posterior vertebral column, outlining the greater sac, lesser sac (omental bursa), greater omentum, lesser omentum, and pelvic peritoneal pouches in sagittal profile.
all.keyConcept: Sagittal section of peritoneum: Displays vertical extent of peritoneal cavity including epiploic foramen, lesser omentum, and recto-vesical/recto-uterine pouches.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Triangular aperture in the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle located superior and lateral to the pubic crest, bounded by the medial and lateral crura and intercrural fibers, transmitting the spermatic cord (or round ligament).
all.keyConcept: Superficial inguinal ring: Triangular defect in external oblique aponeurosis through which the spermatic cord exits the inguinal canal.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Oval opening in the fascia transversalis located approximately 1.25 cm superior to the midinguinal point, immediately lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, representing the interior entrance to the inguinal canal.
all.keyConcept: Deep inguinal ring: Oval opening in fascia transversalis situated lateral to inferior epigastric vessels transmitting structures into inguinal canal.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Cylindrical cord emerging from the superficial inguinal ring and descending into the scrotum, containing the ductus deferens, testicular artery, pampiniform venous plexus, cremasteric artery, and autonomic nerves enclosed in three fascial coats.
all.keyConcept: Spermatic cord: Traverses inguinal canal and exits superficial inguinal ring to suspend the testis; covered by external spermatic, cremasteric, and internal spermatic fascias.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Oblique ~4 cm intramuscular tunnel in the lower anterior abdominal wall running parallel and superior to the medial half of the inguinal ligament between the deep inguinal ring and the superficial inguinal ring.
all.keyConcept: Inguinal canal: ~4 cm oblique passage through lower abdominal wall transmitting the spermatic cord (or round ligament) and ilioinguinal nerve.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large arterial trunk entering the femoral triangle behind the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, situated within the lateral compartment of the femoral sheath, lateral to the femoral vein.
all.keyConcept: Femoral artery: Enters anterior thigh deep to inguinal ligament at midinguinal point, lying lateral to femoral vein within the femoral sheath.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large deep vein ascending through the femoral triangle within the intermediate compartment of the femoral sheath, positioned medial to the femoral artery and lateral to the femoral canal.
all.keyConcept: Femoral vein: Major venous vessel of lower limb ascending in femoral sheath medial to femoral artery before passing deep to inguinal ligament as external iliac vein.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Tag 6 indicates the pubic crest (between the pubic tubercle and pubic symphysis). The muscle originating from the pubic crest and anterior aspect of the pubic symphysis by two tendinous heads is the rectus abdominis muscle.
all.keyConcept: Rectus abdominis: Originates by two heads from pubic crest and pubic symphysis, inserting into costal cartilages 5–7 and xiphoid process.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Tag 2 indicates the outer lip of the iliac crest. The external oblique abdominal muscle inserts by fleshy and aponeurotic fibers into the anterior half of the outer lip of the iliac crest.
all.keyConcept: External oblique muscle: Lower fibers insert into the anterior half of the outer lip of the iliac crest.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Tag 3 indicates the intermediate line of the iliac crest. The internal oblique abdominal muscle originates from the anterior two-thirds of the intermediate line of the iliac crest (as well as lateral two-thirds of inguinal ligament and thoracolumbar fascia).
all.keyConcept: Internal oblique muscle: Originates from the intermediate line of the iliac crest (anterior two-thirds) between outer and inner lips.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Tag 5 indicates both bony attachment sites: the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) laterally and the pubic tubercle medially. The dense fibrous band connecting these two landmarks is the inguinal ligament (Poupart's ligament), formed by the folded lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis.
all.keyConcept: Inguinal ligament (Poupart's): Spans from anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to pubic tubercle as the lower folded border of external oblique aponeurosis.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Tag 4 indicates the sharp, prominent bony ridge on the upper aspect of the superior pubic ramus (pecten pubis), providing attachment for the pectineal (Cooper's) ligament, conjoint tendon, and lacunar ligament.
all.keyConcept: Pectineal line (pecten pubis): Sharp ridge on superior pubic ramus giving attachment to the pectineal ligament and conjoint tendon.

options: Incisive canal and greater palatine vessels
Pterygoid venous plexus and maxillary artery
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Axial and sagittal reformatted contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) images displaying abdominal cross-sections with peritoneal reflections (parietal peritoneum in orange, visceral peritoneum in blue) outlining retroperitoneal and intraperitoneal viscera.
all.keyConcept: Computed Tomography (CT) scan: Cross-sectional radiological imaging using X-ray attenuation to depict peritoneal spaces, retroperitoneum, and abdominal viscera.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The orange dotted outline lines the internal surface of the anterolateral abdominal wall, inferior surface of diaphragm, and pelvic parietes, representing the parietal layer of peritoneum (derived from somatopleuric mesoderm and innervated by somatic nerves).
all.keyConcept: Parietal peritoneum: Lines abdominal and pelvic walls; sensitive to well-localized somatic pain (temperature, touch, pain) via spinal nerves.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The blue continuous outline directly invests and covers the intraperitoneal abdominal viscera (liver, spleen, stomach, small intestine loops), representing the visceral layer of peritoneum (derived from splanchnopleuric mesoderm and innervated by autonomic afferents).
all.keyConcept: Visceral peritoneum: Invests abdominal organs; insensitive to somatic cutting/burning but sensitive to stretch, ischemia, and spasm (referred dull pain).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Dense midline fibrous band formed by the decussation of aponeuroses of the anterolateral abdominal wall muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis), extending vertically from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis between bilateral rectus abdominis muscles.
all.keyConcept: The linea alba is an avascular midline fibrous raphe separating the bilateral rectus abdominis muscles; its lack of major blood vessels makes it a preferred site for median laparotomy.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Triangular or slit-like opening in the aponeurosis of the external abdominal oblique muscle located immediately superior and lateral to the pubic tubercle, bounded by the medial and lateral crura and intercrural fibers.
all.keyConcept: The superficial inguinal ring forms the external exit of the inguinal canal, transmitting the spermatic cord in males (or round ligament of the uterus in females) and the ilioinguinal nerve.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Dense, curved fibrous band formed by the folded-under inferior border of the external abdominal oblique aponeurosis extending from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic tubercle.
all.keyConcept: The inguinal ligament (Poupart's ligament) forms the floor of the inguinal canal and demarcates the anatomical boundary between the anterior abdominal wall and the anterior compartment of the thigh (femoral triangle).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Cylindrical, tubular cord-like structure emerging through the superficial inguinal ring and descending into the scrotum, containing the ductus deferens, testicular and pampiniform vessels, and nerve plexuses wrapped in fascial coverings.
all.keyConcept: The spermatic cord traverses the inguinal canal and acquires coverings from each abdominal wall layer: external spermatic fascia (external oblique), cremasteric muscle and fascia (internal oblique), and internal spermatic fascia (transversalis fascia).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Prominent fibromuscular depression/pucker in the anterior abdominal wall located along the linea alba, corresponding to the obliterated embryonic site of attachment of the umbilical cord.
all.keyConcept: The umbilicus lies typically at the L3–L4 vertebral level, corresponds to the T10 dermatome, and represents an important portosystemic watershed area (where paraumbilical veins anastomose with superficial epigastric veins).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Long, paired, strap-like muscle of the anterior abdominal wall running vertically adjacent to the linea alba from the pubic crest to the xiphoid process and 5th–7th costal cartilages, interrupted by transverse tendinous intersections.
all.keyConcept: Rectus abdominis is the primary flexor of the trunk/lumbar spine and compresses abdominal viscera; it is supplied segmentally by the lower thoracic intercostal and subcostal nerves (T7–T12).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Tough, glistening fibrous sheath covering the anterior surface of the rectus abdominis muscle, formed by the aponeuroses of the flat abdominal wall muscles (external oblique and internal oblique anteriorly).
all.keyConcept: The rectus sheath encloses the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis muscles, along with the superior and inferior epigastric vessels and terminal segments of anterior cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves (T7–T12).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Intermediate flat abdominal wall muscle visible deep to the removed external oblique, characterized by muscle fibers coursing obliquely upward and medially (superomedially) toward the costal margin and rectus sheath.
all.keyConcept: The internal abdominal oblique originates from the thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and lateral inguinal ligament; its lower fibers arch medially with transversus abdominis to form the conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Most superficial of the three flat anterolateral abdominal wall muscles, displaying fleshy digitations arising from the external surfaces of the lower eight ribs with fibers running downward, forward, and medially (inferomedially).
all.keyConcept: External abdominal oblique fibers run inferomedially ('hands in pockets' direction); its aponeurosis contributes to the anterior layer of the rectus sheath and its rolled inferior margin forms the inguinal ligament.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Deepest of the three flat abdominal wall muscles, identified by its horizontally (transversely) oriented muscle fibers situated deep to the internal oblique and leading into a broad medial aponeurosis.
all.keyConcept: Transversus abdominis acts as a natural muscular corset, compressing abdominal contents to increase intra-abdominal pressure during forced expiration, defecation, and micturition.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Intermediate muscle layer of the anterolateral abdominal wall shown in cadaveric dissection deep to the reflected external oblique aponeurosis (pinned laterally), exhibiting fibers passing superomedially toward the rectus sheath.
all.keyConcept: The internal oblique gives origin to cremasteric muscle loops in the spermatic cord and splits its aponeurosis into anterior and posterior laminae to encase the rectus abdominis in its upper three-quarters.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Deepest flat muscle layer exposed through a lateral incision in the internal oblique muscle, featuring characteristic transverse (horizontal) muscle fascicles.
all.keyConcept: Transversus abdominis lies deep to the internal oblique; neurovascular bundles (lower intercostal nerves and vessels) run in the plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Prominent vertical strap muscle of the anterior abdominal wall shown in anatomical dissection both in situ within its sheath on the subject's left and as a reflected flap on the subject's right.
all.keyConcept: The rectus abdominis is firmly adherent to the anterior wall of the rectus sheath at its tendinous intersections, but remains free from the posterior wall, permitting passage of epigastric vessels.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Small, paired, triangular muscle situated superficial to the inferiormost portion of the rectus abdominis within the rectus sheath, originating from the pubic crest and inserting into the inferior linea alba.
all.keyConcept: Pyramidalis tenses the linea alba and is innervated by the subcostal nerve (T12); it is an anatomical landmark for mid-sagittal pubic incisions and is absent in approximately 20% of the population.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Smooth, glistening posterior fibrous wall of the rectus sheath revealed following transection and downward reflection of the rectus abdominis muscle, through which epigastric vessels course.
all.keyConcept: The posterior wall of the rectus sheath ends approximately one-third the distance from the umbilicus to the pubic crest at the crescentic arcuate line, below which rectus abdominis rests directly on transversalis fascia.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Three horizontal, transverse fibrous bands (inscriptiones tendineae) dividing the rectus abdominis into distinct segments and firmly anchoring the muscle to the anterior rectus sheath.
all.keyConcept: Tendinous intersections (typically three: at xiphoid level, umbilicus, and halfway between) represent remnants of embryonic myotomic septa and adhere exclusively to the anterior lamina of the rectus sheath.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Midline vertical fibrous raphe seen extending in the cadaveric dissection between the bilateral rectus abdominis compartments from the xiphoid process down to the pubic symphysis.
all.keyConcept: The linea alba is formed by the interlacing fibers of all three flat lateral abdominal wall aponeuroses; widening or thinning of this structure leads to diastasis recti.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Anatomical structure indicated by its two bony attachments marked on the os coxae: the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) superolaterally and the pubic tubercle inferomedially.
all.keyConcept: The inguinal ligament spans between the ASIS and pubic tubercle; structures passing deep to it include the femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, and iliopsoas muscle.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Distinct angular indentation (incisura cardiaca) formed at the junction between the left border of the abdominal esophagus and the superior curvature (fundus) of the stomach.
all.keyConcept: The cardiac notch creates the angle of His, an anatomical configuration that functions in conjunction with the lower esophageal sphincter as a mechanical barrier preventing gastroesophageal reflux.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Long, expansive, convex lateral and inferior border of the stomach marked along its course from the cardiac notch to the pylorus.
all.keyConcept: The greater curvature gives attachment to the gastrosplenic ligament superiorly and the greater omentum along its inferior span; it is vascularized by the short gastric, left gastro-omental, and right gastro-omental arteries.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red highlighted line marks the shorter, concave right and superior border of the stomach extending from the cardiac orifice to the pylorus, which provides attachment to the lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments).
all.keyConcept: The lesser curvature forms the concave postero-superior/right border of the stomach and gives attachment to the lesser omentum; it contains the incisura angularis and is supplied by the anastomosing right and left gastric arteries.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the distal, tubular, narrow segment (approximately 2–3 cm long) of the pyloric region of the stomach that leads directly into the duodenum at the pyloric constriction.
all.keyConcept: The pyloric region is divided into a wider proximal pyloric antrum and a narrower distal pyloric canal; the canal ends at the pyloric sphincter (gastroduodenal junction).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the broad, expanded proximal chamber of the pyloric region located between the incisura angularis (demarcating the body) and the distal tubular pyloric canal.
all.keyConcept: The pyloric antrum is the wider proximal division of the pyloric part of the stomach; it contains endocrine G-cells secreting gastrin and produces forceful peristaltic mixing waves.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow identifies the central, largest region of the stomach situated between the horizontal plane through the cardiac notch (separating the fundus above) and the oblique plane through the angular incisure (separating the pyloric antrum below).
all.keyConcept: The body of the stomach represents its largest anatomical division, lined by prominent rugae and containing gastric glands rich in parietal (oxyntic) and chief (peptic) cells.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red line highlights the greater curvature of the stomach, which serves as the site of attachment for the greater omentum, an extensive double sheet of peritoneum (four layers) derived embryologically from the dorsal mesentery (dorsal mesogastrium).
all.keyConcept: The greater omentum suspends from the greater curvature of the stomach and transverse colon, derived from the dorsal mesentery; it wraps around intra-abdominal inflammatory foci ('policeman of the abdomen').

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red line highlights the lesser curvature of the stomach, which gives attachment to the lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments), derived embryologically from the ventral mesentery (ventral mesogastrium).
all.keyConcept: The lesser omentum connects the lesser curvature of the stomach and the first part of the duodenum to the liver; derived from embryonic ventral mesentery, its free margin encloses the portal triad.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the uncinate process, a hook-shaped projection extending medially and superiorly from the inferior part of the head of the pancreas, situated posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
all.keyConcept: The uncinate process of the pancreas develops from the ventral pancreatic bud; it extends medially behind the superior mesenteric vessels (SMA and SMV) and rests posteriorly on the abdominal aorta.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the head of the pancreas, the expanded disc-shaped right extremity of the pancreas firmly nestled within the C-shaped concavity of the duodenum.
all.keyConcept: The head of the pancreas lies within the C-loop of the duodenum anterior to the IVC and renal veins; tumors here frequently compress the common bile duct, causing painless obstructive jaundice.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the constricted neck of the pancreas (about 2 cm in length) connecting the head to the body, lying directly anterior to the superior mesenteric vessels and origin of the portal vein.
all.keyConcept: The neck of the pancreas bridges the head and body; posteriorly, the superior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein directly behind the pancreatic neck.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the elongated, prismatic body of the pancreas extending obliquely to the left across the abdominal aorta, L2 vertebra, and left kidney towards the spleen.
all.keyConcept: The body of the pancreas forms part of the stomach bed, separated from the stomach by the lesser sac (omental bursa); the splenic artery runs tortuously along its superior border.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the narrow, tapered left tip of the pancreas, which extends into the splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament to reach the hilum of the spleen.
all.keyConcept: The tail of the pancreas is the only intraperitoneal part of the organ, situated within the splenorenal ligament alongside the splenic vessels; it contains the highest relative density of islets of Langerhans.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The black arrow enters the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow), the natural aperture communicating between the greater peritoneal sac and the lesser sac (omental bursa), situated directly posterior to the free right margin of the lesser omentum.
all.keyConcept: The epiploic foramen is bounded anteriorly by the portal triad (bile duct, hepatic artery proper, portal vein) in the hepatoduodenal ligament, posteriorly by the IVC, superiorly by the caudate lobe of the liver, and inferiorly by the first part of the duodenum.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The teal arrow (label 11) points to the anal canal, the terminal 3–4 cm of the large intestine extending from the anorectal junction through the pelvic diaphragm/perineum to the external anal orifice.
all.keyConcept: The anal canal begins at the anorectal junction where the rectum pierces the levator ani; it features the pectinate line dividing neurovascular and lymphatic drainage into somatic and visceral territories.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The teal arrow (label 10) points to the rectum, the pelvic portion of the large intestine between the sigmoid colon (at S3 level) and the anal canal, characterized by a smooth external surface lacking haustra, taeniae, or appendices epiploicae.
all.keyConcept: The rectum extends from S3 to the pelvic diaphragm; it possesses three lateral curvatures marked internally by transverse rectal folds (valves of Houston) and dilates inferiorly to form the rectal ampulla.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 2 points to the vermiform appendix, a narrow, blind-ended tubular diverticulum originating from the posteromedial caecal wall at the convergence of the three taeniae coli, approximately 2 cm below the ileocaecal valve.
all.keyConcept: The vermiform appendix contains abundant lymphoid follicles in its submucosa and is suspended by the mesoappendix carrying the appendicular artery (a branch of the ileocolic artery); its anatomical base is reliably found at the confluence of the three taeniae coli.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 1 points to the terminal ileum as it approaches and enters the medial wall of the caecum at the ileocaecal junction.
all.keyConcept: The terminal ileum enters the caecum at the ileocaecal junction, flanked by superior and inferior ileocaecal lips that form the ileocaecal valve, regulating emptying and preventing retrograde colonic reflux.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 1 points to loops of jejunum located predominantly in the upper left infragolic compartment; corroborated by the inset displaying prominent, dense circular mucosal folds (plicae circulares), simple arterial arcades (1–2 tiers), and long straight vasa recta.
all.keyConcept: The jejunum comprises the proximal two-fifths of the small intestine following the duodenum; characterized by a wider caliber, thicker wall, prominent plicae circulares, tall vasa recta, and less mesenteric fat compared to the ileum.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 2 points to loops of ileum situated primarily in the lower right infragolic compartment and pelvis; corroborated by the inset showing multiple complex arterial arcade tiers (3–4 tiers), short vasa recta, abundant mesenteric fat encroaching onto the intestinal border, and sparse plicae circulares.
all.keyConcept: The ileum forms the distal three-fifths of the small intestine; distinguished by abundant mesenteric fat extending up to the intestinal wall, short vasa recta arising from multi-tiered arcades, and aggregated lymphoid nodules (Peyer's patches).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 7 points to the transverse mesocolon, the broad peritoneal fold connecting the transverse colon to the posterior abdominal wall along the anterior border of the pancreas.
all.keyConcept: The transverse mesocolon conveys the middle colic vessels to the transverse colon; its horizontal root divides the abdominal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 6 points to the greater omentum, shown here reflected superiorly over the costal margin; it is the extensive peritoneal apron attached to the greater curvature of the stomach and transverse colon.
all.keyConcept: The greater omentum is a four-layered fold of peritoneum containing fat and milky spots (macrophage aggregates); it drapes over the small intestine and adheres to inflamed areas to prevent peritonitis.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The caecum is the blind-ended intestinal pouch situated in the right iliac fossa inferior to the ileocecal junction. It is characterized by three distinct taeniae coli converging at the posteromedial base of the vermiform appendix, sacculations (haustrations), and complete peritoneal covering without a true mesentery.
all.keyConcept: The caecum occupies the right iliac fossa below the ileocecal opening and serves as the convergence point for all three taeniae coli at the appendiceal base.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The ascending colon is the secondarily retroperitoneal segment of the large intestine extending vertically upward through the right flank and right lumbar region from the caecum to the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver, continuing into the right colic flexure.
all.keyConcept: The ascending colon is fixed to the posterior abdominal wall (secondarily retroperitoneal) and ascends from the caecum to the hepatic flexure.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The sigmoid colon is the mobile, S-shaped intraperitoneal loop of large bowel suspended by the fan-shaped sigmoid mesocolon, extending from the pelvic brim (in continuation with the descending colon) to the third sacral vertebra (S3), where it terminates at the rectum.
all.keyConcept: The sigmoid colon is an intraperitoneal loop with a distinct mesentery and numerous appendices epiploicae, transitioning into the rectum at the level of S3.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The right colic (hepatic) flexure is the acute right-angled bend connecting the ascending colon to the transverse colon in the right hypochondrium. It lies directly inferior to the visceral surface of the right lobe of the liver (producing the colic impression) and anterior to the lower pole of the right kidney, positioned inferior to the left colic flexure.
all.keyConcept: The right colic flexure marks the transition from ascending to transverse colon beneath the right lobe of the liver and lies lower than the splenic flexure.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The transverse colon is the longest and most mobile intraperitoneal segment of the large intestine, spanning horizontally across the abdomen from the right colic flexure to the left colic flexure, completely suspended from the posterior abdominal wall by the transverse mesocolon.
all.keyConcept: The transverse colon crosses the abdominal cavity suspended by the transverse mesocolon and receives dual arterial supply from both the SMA and IMA.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The left colic (splenic) flexure is the sharp junction between the transverse colon and descending colon in the left hypochondrium. It lies against the visceral surface of the spleen and lower pole of the left kidney, anchored securely to the diaphragm by the phrenicocolic ligament and positioned higher and more posterior than the right colic flexure.
all.keyConcept: The left colic (splenic) flexure is situated higher and more posteriorly than the hepatic flexure, supported by the phrenicocolic ligament.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The descending colon is the secondarily retroperitoneal segment of the large intestine passing vertically downward along the left posterior abdominal wall from the left colic flexure to the pelvic inlet, where it curves medially to become the sigmoid colon.
all.keyConcept: The descending colon is secondarily retroperitoneal, narrower in caliber than the ascending colon, and supplied primarily by the left colic artery from the IMA.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The atypical fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) is characterized by very massive, short, thick, conical/pyramidal transverse processes that are attached to both the pedicle and the lateral surface of the vertebral body, and by a large vertebral body with greater anterior than posterior vertical height.
all.keyConcept: L5 is an atypical lumbar vertebra distinguished by its massive transverse processes attached continuously across both the pedicle and the vertebral body.

options: Typical L5 vertebra as it short, thick, attached to pedicle & body
Atypical L5 vertebra as it short, thick, attached to pedicle & body
Typical L3 vertebra as it short, thick, attached to pedicle & body
Atypical L1 vertebra as it long, thin, attached to pedicle
Typical L4 vertebra as it long, thin, attached to pedicle
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Typical lumbar vertebrae (L1–L4) feature long, thin, slender, horizontally directed transverse processes that arise solely from the junction of the pedicle and lamina (without any attachment to the vertebral body), a large kidney-shaped body, and a triangular vertebral foramen.
all.keyConcept: Typical lumbar vertebrae (L1–L4) are recognized by slender transverse processes attached strictly to the neural arch/pedicle junction rather than the body.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The specimen exhibits all hallmarks of typical lumbar vertebrae (L1–L4), including a reniform (kidney-shaped) body, triangular vertebral foramen, slender elongated transverse processes originating at the junction of pedicles and laminae, vertically oriented articular facets, and a horizontal hatchet-shaped spinous process.
all.keyConcept: Lumbar vertebrae L1 through L4 are typical lumbar vertebrae, whereas L5 is an atypical vertebra.

all.text: Which of the following true about this vertebra
options: Short, thick pyramidal, attached to both pedicle & body
Long, thin, attached to pedicle & body
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The arrow indicates the pedicle of a typical lumbar vertebra, which is a short, stout, cylindrical bar of bone projecting straight posteriorly from the upper portion of the posterolateral aspect of the kidney-shaped vertebral body.
all.keyConcept: The pedicles of typical lumbar vertebrae are strong, short bony struts that form the lateral boundaries of the triangular vertebral foramen.

all.text: Which of the following true about this vertebra
options: Short, thick pyramidal, attached to both pedicle & body
Long, thin, attached to pedicle & body
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrows point to the transverse processes of the atypical L5 vertebra, which are characteristically short, thick, and pyramidal in shape, and firmly anchored to both the pedicle and the lateral surface of the vertebral body to resist anterior shear forces and transmit load to the pelvis.
all.keyConcept: The transverse process of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) is uniquely short, thick, pyramidal, and attached to both the pedicle and vertebral body.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The symbols mark the central opening (vertebral foramen) within the vertebra, which is distinctly triangular in the lumbar region and contributes to the continuous vertebral canal housing the cauda equina, filum terminale, and spinal meninges.
all.keyConcept: The lumbar vertebral foramen is triangular in cross-section and forms the vertebral canal that transmits the cauda equina.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the mammillary process, a distinct rounded tubercle situated on the posterior margin of the superior articular process of a lumbar vertebra, serving as an attachment site for deep back muscles (multifidus and medial intertransversarii).
all.keyConcept: The mammillary process is a characteristic anatomical feature of lumbar vertebrae located on the posterior border of each superior articular process.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the accessory process, a small bony projection found on the posterior aspect of the base (root) of the transverse process in lumbar vertebrae, serving as an insertion point for the intertransversarii and longissimus muscles.
all.keyConcept: The accessory process is located on the posterior aspect of the root of the transverse process, distinguishing it from the mammillary process on the superior articular process.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The arrows indicate the smooth, concave articular facet on the superior articular process of the lumbar vertebra, which is vertically oriented and faces medially and slightly posteriorly in the sagittal plane to interlock with the inferior articular facet of the superior adjacent vertebra.
all.keyConcept: Lumbar superior articular facets are vertically oriented, concave, and face posteromedially to resist rotation while allowing flexion and extension.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow in this lateral view of articulated lumbar vertebrae points to the inferior articular facet, which projects downward from the junction of the pedicle and lamina and presents a smooth, convex articular surface directed anterolaterally.
all.keyConcept: Lumbar inferior articular facets project inferiorly and face anterolaterally, fitting between the medially facing superior articular facets of the vertebra below.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The arrows point to the spinous process (spine) of the lumbar vertebra, which is a broad, sturdy, quadrilateral (hatchet-shaped) plate of bone projecting horizontally backward from the junction of the two laminae in the posterior midline.
all.keyConcept: The lumbar spinous process is stout, horizontally directed, and quadrilateral, facilitating dorsal access to the vertebral canal for lumbar punctures.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The arrows point to the vertebral lamina, a broad, thick, flattened plate of bone extending posteromedially from the pedicle and articular processes to unite in the midline with its fellow from the opposite side, forming the posterior wall of the vertebral canal and the base of the spinous process.
all.keyConcept: The lumbar laminae are broad, robust bony plates forming the posterior arch of the vertebra and serving as attachment sites for the ligamentum flavum.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The arrows point to the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae, which project laterally from the vertebral arch (slender and elongated in typical vertebrae; thick and conical in atypical L5), functioning as leverage arms for muscular and ligamentous attachments.
all.keyConcept: Lumbar transverse processes represent costal elements projecting laterally from the junction of the pedicle and lamina (or pedicle and body in L5).

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow indicates the vertebral body (corpus vertebrae), the large, kidney-shaped anterior weight-bearing segment of the lumbar vertebra with a perforated, cribriform superior articular surface bounded by a smooth epiphysial ring.
all.keyConcept: The vertebral body forms the robust, anterior weight-bearing component of each vertebra, supporting axial loads and articulating with adjacent bodies via fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the cribriform superior articular surface of the lumbar vertebral body, which is lined by a thin plate of hyaline cartilage and serves as the direct attachment site for the fibrocartilaginous intervertebral disc.
all.keyConcept: Intervertebral discs form secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses) between the superior and inferior articular surfaces of adjacent vertebral bodies, providing shock absorption and tensile strength.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points directly to the posterior tip (apex) of the spinous process of the lumbar vertebra, which provides attachment to the supraspinous ligament.
all.keyConcept: The supraspinous ligament attaches to the tips of the spinous processes from vertebra C7 to the sacrum, connecting adjacent spines and limiting hyperflexion of the vertebral column.

all.text: Mention Structure Attached to blue marker
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The blue marker highlights the border/margin of the spinous process extending between the root and apex, which provides attachment for the interspinous ligament connecting adjacent spinous processes.
all.keyConcept: Interspinous ligaments are thin membranous bands connecting adjacent spinous processes along their margins, blending posteriorly with the supraspinous ligament and anteriorly with the ligamenta flava.

all.text: Mention Structure Attached to blue marker
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The blue marker is placed along the anterior surface and lower border of the transverse process of the lumbar vertebra, representing the posterior (deep) slip of origin of the psoas major muscle.
all.keyConcept: Psoas major arises from the anterior surfaces and lower borders of the transverse processes of all lumbar vertebrae (L1–L5), as well as from the lateral surfaces of the T12–L5 vertebral bodies and intervening intervertebral discs.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: In this lateral view schematic of a lumbar vertebra, label 'A' indicates the lateral aspect of the vertebral body between the upper and lower margins, where the main slips and tendinous arches of the psoas major muscle arise across the constricted waist of the body.
all.keyConcept: Psoas major originates via muscular slips from the margins of the lumbar vertebral bodies and discs, bridged by tendinous arches spanning across the middle of each body over the lumbar vessels.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: In this lateral view schematic of a lumbar vertebra, label 'B' designates the lumbar transverse process, corresponding to the insertion of the quadratus lumborum muscle (listed in options as 'Insertion of quadratus lamborum').
all.keyConcept: Quadratus lumborum inserts into the transverse processes of the upper lumbar vertebrae (L1–L4) and the inferior border of the 12th rib, stabilizing the lumbar spine and depressing the ribcage.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label '2' marks the broad green band covering the anterior aspect of the vertebral body, designating the anterior longitudinal ligament.
all.keyConcept: The anterior longitudinal ligament is a strong, broad fibrous band covering and connecting the anterior and anterolateral surfaces of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs, preventing hyperextension of the vertebral column.

all.text: Structure Attached To Blue Marked Area
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The blue highlighted area is positioned on the posterior surface of the vertebral body forming the anterior wall of the vertebral canal, the exact attachment site of the posterior longitudinal ligament.
all.keyConcept: The posterior longitudinal ligament extends along the posterior surfaces of the vertebral bodies within the vertebral canal from C2 down to the sacrum, resisting hyperflexion and helping prevent posterior disc herniation.

all.text: Mention Structure Attached to blue marker
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The blue marker specifically covers the apex (tip) of the transverse process of the lumbar vertebra, the definitive skeletal site where fibers of the quadratus lumborum muscle insert (listed in options as 'Insertion of quadratus lamborum').
all.keyConcept: Quadratus lumborum inserts into the tips of the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae (L1–L4) and the lower border of the 12th rib, acting as an ipsilateral lateral flexor of the trunk.

all.text: Mention Structure related to blue marker
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The blue oval lies immediately anterior to the right side of the body of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5), corresponding to the inferior vena cava (IVC) which is formed at this anatomical level by the confluence of the right and left common iliac veins.
all.keyConcept: The inferior vena cava (IVC) begins on the right anterior aspect of the L5 vertebral body where the right and left common iliac veins unite behind the right common iliac artery.

all.text: Mention Structure Attached to red marker
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red markers are placed on the tips of the massive, pyramidal transverse processes of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5), which provide attachment to the stout iliolumbar ligament.
all.keyConcept: The iliolumbar ligament connects the transverse process of the L5 vertebra to the inner lip of the iliac crest, stabilizing the lumbosacral junction against forward translation and torsion.

all.text: What is the type of marked "2" joint
all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The joint indicated by label '2' (circled in yellow) is the zygapophysial (facet) joint between the inferior articular process of the superior vertebra and the superior articular process of the inferior vertebra, classified structurally as a plane synovial joint.
all.keyConcept: Zygapophysial (facet) joints are plane synovial joints with hyaline cartilage articular facets that guide and restrict the movements of the vertebral column.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 1 indicates the psoas minor muscle, recognized by its slender, thin muscle belly and long glistening tendon coursing down the anterior aspect of the psoas major to insert onto the pectineal line and iliopubic eminence.
all.keyConcept: Psoas minor lies directly on the anterior surface of the psoas major and inserts on the iliopubic eminence; it is absent in approximately 40% of individuals.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 2 indicates the psoas major, the large, thick fusiform retroperitoneal muscle originating from the lumbar vertebrae and descending along the pelvic brim to pass deep to the inguinal ligament into the lesser trochanter.
all.keyConcept: Psoas major is the chief flexor of the thigh at the hip joint and forms the lateral boundary of the pelvic brim, enclosed within the tubular psoas fascia.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 3 indicates the quadratus lumborum muscle (spelled 'Quadratus lumboru' in the options), a quadrilateral muscular sheet occupying the posterior abdominal wall lateral to the psoas major between the iliac crest below and the 12th rib above.
all.keyConcept: Quadratus lumborum forms a major component of the posterior abdominal wall, fixes the 12th rib during forced inspiration, and produces lateral flexion of the vertebral column.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 4 indicates the iliacus muscle, recognized by its broad, fan-shaped morphology lining the iliac fossa of the pelvic bone, converging with the psoas major tendon to insert into the lesser trochanter.
all.keyConcept: Iliacus fills the iliac fossa and joins the psoas major to form the iliopsoas muscle, the primary and most powerful flexor of the hip joint.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 1 indicates the abdominal aorta, the prominent midline retroperitoneal arterial trunk descending anterior to the lumbar vertebral column to the left of the IVC, bifurcating at the L4 level.
all.keyConcept: The abdominal aorta begins at the T12 aortic hiatus of the diaphragm and terminates at the L4 vertebral level by dividing into the right and left common iliac arteries.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 2 indicates the inferior vena cava (IVC), the massive systemic venous trunk situated on the posterior abdominal wall to the right of the abdominal aorta and vertebral column.
all.keyConcept: The IVC is formed at the L5 vertebral level by the confluence of the common iliac veins and ascends to pierce the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T8 level.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 3 indicates the left common iliac artery, arising from the terminal bifurcation of the abdominal aorta at the L4 level and descending inferolaterally toward the pelvic brim where it divides into internal and external iliac branches.
all.keyConcept: The common iliac arteries arise from the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta at L4 and divide into the external and internal iliac arteries anterior to the sacroiliac joint.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large venous channel situated in the lower lumbar and pelvic region, formed by the confluence of the external and internal iliac veins anterior to the sacroiliac joint. The left common iliac vein ascends obliquely medial to the left common iliac artery and crosses posterior to the right common iliac artery to unite with the right common iliac vein at L5, forming the inferior vena cava (IVC).
all.keyConcept: Common iliac vein: Formed by internal and external iliac veins; the left common iliac vein crosses posterior to the right common iliac artery at L5 to join the IVC.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the anterior ramus of the T12 thoracic spinal nerve. It enters the posterior abdominal wall behind the lateral arcuate ligament of the diaphragm and runs obliquely downward and laterally along the lower border of the 12th rib across the anterior surface of the quadratus lumborum muscle, superior to the iliohypogastric nerve.
all.keyConcept: Subcostal nerve (T12): Descends below the 12th rib across the upper quadratus lumborum to innervate the anterior abdominal wall muscles and overlying skin.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the anterior ramus of the L1 spinal nerve. It emerges from the upper lateral border of the psoas major muscle superior to the ilioinguinal nerve, crosses obliquely downward and laterally across the quadratus lumborum muscle toward the iliac crest, and pierces the transversus abdominis to supply hypogastric skin and lower abdominal wall muscles.
all.keyConcept: Iliohypogastric nerve (L1): Emerges from the upper lateral border of psoas major above the ilioinguinal nerve, crossing quadratus lumborum to innervate suprapubic skin and abdominal muscles.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the anterior ramus of the L1 spinal nerve. It emerges from the lateral border of the psoas major muscle immediately inferior to the iliohypogastric nerve, traverses the quadratus lumborum and iliacus muscles near the iliac crest, enters the inguinal canal, and traverses the superficial inguinal ring to provide cutaneous sensation to the upper medial thigh and external genitalia.
all.keyConcept: Ilioinguinal nerve (L1): Emerges from the lateral border of psoas major below the iliohypogastric nerve, traverses the inguinal canal, and exits through the superficial ring.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the posterior divisions of the L2 and L3 anterior rami. It emerges from the lateral border of the psoas major muscle, courses obliquely downward and laterally across the iliacus muscle toward the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS), and passes deep to the lateral end of the inguinal ligament to enter the anterolateral thigh.
all.keyConcept: Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh (L2–L3): Crosses the iliacus muscle toward the ASIS and passes deep to the inguinal ligament; compression causes meralgia paresthetica.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the anterior divisions of the L2, L3, and L4 anterior rami within the psoas major muscle. It is the sole branch of the lumbar plexus that emerges from the MEDIAL border of the psoas major muscle, crossing the pelvic brim into the lesser pelvis and heading through the obturator canal to supply the medial (adductor) compartment of the thigh.
all.keyConcept: Obturator nerve (L2–L4): The only lumbar plexus branch emerging from the medial border of psoas major; enters the obturator canal to innervate thigh adductors.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus, arising from the posterior divisions of the L2, L3, and L4 anterior rami. It emerges from the lower lateral border of the psoas major muscle and descends in the groove between the psoas major and iliacus muscles deep to the iliac fascia, passing behind the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery into the femoral triangle.
all.keyConcept: Femoral nerve (L2–L4): Descends in the groove between psoas major and iliacus muscles, entering the femoral triangle lateral to the femoral sheath to supply anterior thigh muscles.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from the L1 and L2 anterior rami within the psoas major muscle. Its diagnostic anatomical hallmark is that it pierces the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle and descends vertically on its anterior fascia, dividing into genital (supplying cremaster muscle and scrotal/labial skin) and femoral branches.
all.keyConcept: Genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2): Pierces and runs on the anterior surface of psoas major; its genital branch supplies the cremaster muscle mediating the cremasteric reflex.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Sickle-shaped peritoneal reflection attached to the anterior and superior (diaphragmatic) surfaces of the liver and to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm, separating the anatomical right and left lobes.
all.keyConcept: The falciform ligament connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall; its free inferior margin contains the ligamentum teres hepatis (obliterated left umbilical vein) and small paraumbilical veins.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Green pear-shaped hollow sac situated on the visceral surface of the liver in the gallbladder fossa, with its fundus projecting beyond the sharp inferior border.
all.keyConcept: The fundus of the gallbladder typically projects beyond the inferior border of the liver at the transpyloric plane, where the lateral border of the rectus abdominis intersects the 9th right costal cartilage.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large, dominant anatomical lobe lying to the right of the falciform ligament on the diaphragmatic surface, contributing roughly five-sixths of the total hepatic volume.
all.keyConcept: Anatomically, the right lobe of the liver is demarcated anteriorly by the falciform ligament, but functionally (Couinaud segmentation), the true functional right liver begins to the right of Cantlie's line.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Flattened, wedge-shaped anatomical lobe lying to the left of the falciform ligament on the anterior/diaphragmatic surface of the liver.
all.keyConcept: The anatomical left lobe lies to the left of the falciform ligament and fissure for ligamentum venosum, corresponding to Couinaud segments II and III.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Deep transverse fissure on the visceral surface of the liver, bounded anteriorly by the quadrate lobe and posteriorly by the caudate lobe, transmitting the portal triad structures.
all.keyConcept: The porta hepatis serves as the hilum of the liver, transmitting the hepatic portal vein (posteriorly), hepatic artery proper (anterior-left), and bile ducts (anterior-right), enveloped in Glisson's capsule.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Centrally located transverse hepatic hilum fissure between the caudate process/lobe above and quadrate lobe below, conveying the portal vein, hepatic artery branches, and hepatic bile ducts.
all.keyConcept: The porta hepatis forms the horizontal crossbar of the 'H-shaped' visceral surface of the liver and transmits the components of the portal triad within the free margin of the lesser omentum.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Anterior-inferior longitudinal groove situated on the visceral surface between the left anatomical lobe and the quadrate lobe, housing the obliterated umbilical vein.
all.keyConcept: The fissure for ligamentum teres forms the anterior part of the left longitudinal limb of the hepatic 'H' groove, extending from the inferior border of the liver to the left end of the porta hepatis.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Distinct, rectangular lobe situated on the posterosuperior visceral surface between the fissure for ligamentum venosum (left) and groove for IVC (right), superior to the porta hepatis.
all.keyConcept: The caudate lobe (Spigelian lobe / Couinaud segment I) receives vascular branches from both right and left portal triads and drains directly into the IVC via small independent hepatic veins.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Four-sided (rectangular) lobe on the inferior visceral surface, bounded by the fossa for gallbladder on the right, fissure for ligamentum teres on the left, and porta hepatis posteriorly.
all.keyConcept: Though anatomically part of the right lobe of the liver, the quadrate lobe functionally belongs to the left liver (Couinaud segment IV) because it receives blood supply from the left hepatic artery and left branch of the portal vein.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Vertical sulcus situated on the posterior surface between the caudate lobe and bare area of the right lobe, accommodating the inferior vena cava.
all.keyConcept: The groove for the IVC forms the posterior part of the right longitudinal limb of the visceral 'H'; hepatic veins emerge here directly to empty into the inferior vena cava.

all.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large non-peritoneal triangular area on the posterior/diaphragmatic surface of the right lobe of the liver, bounded by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament.
